exam: A 25‑year‑old male develops severe muscle rigidity and temperature 39 °C after halothane – what is your immediate management? — Give dantrolene, cool, support ventilation, monitor CK and electrolytes.
Explain how a phospholamban mutation could present clinically. — Reduced SERCA activity → prolonged contraction, possible heart failure signs, especially in high‑output states.

Differentiate malignant hyperthermia from neuroleptic malignant syndrome at the bedside. — MH: anesthesia trigger, rapid rise in CO2, hyperkalemia; NMS: antipsychotic use, slower onset, prominent mental status change.
What laboratory test confirms malignant hyperthermia susceptibility and what if it is unavailable? — CHCT; if unavailable, rely on family history and clinical reaction.
A patient with known RYR1 mutation needs surgery – what anesthetic plan do you choose? — Use total intravenous anesthesia without volatile agents or succinylcholine; have dantrolene ready.
How does ATP depletion in sepsis affect the SR and muscle function? — Impaired SERCA activity leads to calcium accumulation in cytosol, causing weakness and possible contracture.
Describe the triad structure and its relevance to excitation‑contraction coupling. — T‑tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae; ensures rapid calcium release to all myofibrils.
Why might CK be normal early in malignant hyperthermia and how should you act? — CK rises after muscle breakdown; treat based on clinical signs, do not wait for CK.
ai.title: Sarcoplasmic Reticulum in Skeletal Muscle
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) stores calcium for rapid release during contraction and re‑uptake for relaxation. Understanding its function helps diagnose and manage disorders of muscle tone and calcium handling, especially where advanced tests are limited.

b: Extensive network in fast‑twitch fibers
Contains calsequestrin for high‑capacity Ca2+ binding
Works with dihydropyridine receptors (DHPR) on T‑tubules
sections.p: The SR is a specialised endoplasmic reticulum network surrounding each myofibril. It forms terminal cisternae at the triad, linking to T‑tubules for excitation‑contraction coupling.

b: Ca2+ release → contraction
SERCA pump re‑uptakes Ca2+ → relaxation
ATP required for SERCA activity
sections.p: An action potential travels down the T‑tubule, activating DHPR which mechanically opens ryanodine receptors (RyR1) on the SR, releasing Ca2+ into the cytosol. Calcium binds troponin, allowing cross‑bridge cycling.

b: Phosphorylation relieves phospholamban inhibition
Low ATP → impaired re‑uptake, prolonged contraction
sections.p: SERCA activity is modulated by phospholamban (inhibited when dephosphorylated) and by sarcolipin. Hormonal signals (e.g., catecholamines) increase cAMP, enhancing SERCA via PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban.

b: Malignant hyperthermia – uncontrolled Ca2+ release
Central core disease – RyR1 mutation, reduced Ca2+ release
Hypocalcemia – limited SR calcium pool, weak contraction
sections.p: Defects in SR calcium handling produce muscle weakness, cramps, or malignant hyperthermia. Genetic mutations in RyR1 or CACNA1S alter channel gating; acquired depletion of ATP (e.g., severe sepsis) impairs SERCA.

b: Trigger avoidance (volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine)
Prompt dantrolene administration
Monitor core temperature, CK, and electrolytes
sections.p: Recognising SR disorders guides emergency management (e.g., dantrolene for malignant hyperthermia) and informs peri‑operative planning for patients with known susceptibility.

t.b: Is there muscle breakdown? Elevated CK supports rhabdomyolysis or malignant hyperthermia.
Does the patient have malignant hyperthermia susceptibility? Positive contracture confirms RyR1 defect.
Identifies inherited SR channel mutations. Positive result confirms diagnosis and informs relatives.

b: Dantrolene – blocks RyR1 Ca2+ release; first‑line for malignant hyperthermia
IV fluids and cooling – prevent renal failure from rhabdomyolysis
Correct electrolytes (K+, Ca2+) and maintain glucose
Avoid triggering agents in future surgeries
sections.p: Treat the trigger, then support muscle relaxation and metabolic stability.

b: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – drug‑induced dopamine blockade, not SR dysfunction
Septic shock – hyperthermia from cytokines, not calcium release
Normal CK early in malignant hyperthermia may give false reassurance
Genetic testing may miss rare variants; clinical suspicion remains crucial

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid rise in core temperature > 38.5 °C after anesthesia
Muscle rigidity with hypercarbia and acidosis
Sudden unexplained cardiac arrhythmia with high CK
